extracted.intended_audience: scientists, researchers, and science communicators (AAAS members and researchers considering public engagement)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and practicing public engagement with science that is intentional, mutual, and inclusive; explains goals, benefits, barriers, and approaches for scientists engaging public audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional, meaningful interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public engagement with science describes intentional, meaningful interactions that provide opportunities for mutual learning between scientists and members of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize purposefulness ('intentional') and depth ('meaningful') rather than ad hoc or purely promotional interactions. Interactions should be designed to enable two-way exchange rather than one-way transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual learning refers not just to the acquisition of knowledge, but also to increased familiarity with a breadth of perspectives, frames, and worldviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success not only by facts conveyed but by whether scientists and publics learn from each other and gain appreciation for differing perspectives and frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic engagement skills and empowerment as goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals for public engagement with science in addition to mutual learning include civic engagement skills and empowerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that build participants' capacity to engage civically (e.g., deliberation, advocacy, participation in decision-making) and that foster empowerment rather than passive receipt of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased awareness of cultural relevance of science
rubrics_metrics.description: A goal is increased awareness of the cultural relevance of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame engagement to highlight how science connects to cultural contexts and everyday life, making it more salient and relevant to diverse publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of multiple perspectives and knowledge domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the importance of multiple perspectives and domains of knowledge to scientific endeavors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value non-scientific ways of knowing and include a range of expertise and lived experiences in engagement design and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive platform for stakeholder interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interaction between interested stakeholders is critical to finding common ground on scientific issues affecting society; public engagement can provide a constructive platform for public views to be combined with scientific expertise in decision-making contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use engagement to surface and integrate stakeholder views into decision contexts; design formats that enable constructive exchange even when tensions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move beyond one-way public understanding to two-way engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The public engagement approach often uses and builds on public understanding efforts, while moving toward more comprehensive and interactive opportunities for dialogue and exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dialogic formats (Q&A, deliberative panels, workshops) over one-way lectures when the goal is addressing concerns, benefits, and tradeoffs; engagement should be interactive and reciprocal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss benefits and risks openly
rubrics_metrics.description: Through engagement, scientists and the public participate in discussions about the benefits and risks of the science and technology impacting our daily lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conversations explicitly address both benefits and risks, and create space for public questions and concerns to be raised and addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve a wide range of interested stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Involving a wide range of interested stakeholders can connect seemingly unrelated viewpoints, with potentially far-reaching effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recruit diverse stakeholders (communities, practitioners, policy actors) to broaden perspectives and identify intersections across viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand reach and societal relevance of scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists can expand the reach of their work, and make it more relevant to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use engagement to broaden audience reach and to surface societal needs and applications that make research more relevant and impactful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for research and professional benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing body of work suggests scientists benefit from engaging with the public; engagement may help meet grant requirements and increase scientific impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame engagement as professionally valuable: it can satisfy funding agency broader-impact requirements (e.g., NSF) and correlates with increased visibility/impact, including via social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate and recognize engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrating the work of respected scientists who engage public audiences may catalyze wider, more explicit recognition of the value of public engagement (e.g., AAAS awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal recognition (awards, honors) to incentivize and legitimize engagement within the scientific community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and plan for common barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists report barriers to engaging public audiences, notably time and a concern that it will shift attention from their research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate constraints such as limited time and perceived trade-offs with research productivity; explicitly address these when proposing engagement activities and workload planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate barriers via partnerships with engagement practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnerships with public engagement practitioners, such as an outreach director or event organizer, can minimize the time required for a scientist’s engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborate with communications/outreach professionals to share logistics and design work; delegate event organization to reduce burden on researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many approaches to get started
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many approaches to public engagement and several entry points for scientists to begin engaging public audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible: choose methods appropriate to goals, audiences, and constraints (e.g., lectures, dialogues, social media, partnerships); seek AAAS resources and examples to find suitable formats.
